      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt1">Eczema</span> is a term for several different types of skin swelling. <span class="qt1">Eczema</span> is also called <span class="qt0">dermatitis</span>. Most types cause dry, itchy skin and <span class="qt2">rashes</span> on the face, inside the elbows and behind the knees, and on the hands and feet. Scratching the skin can cause it to turn red, and to swell and itch even more.</p><p><span class="qt1">Eczema</span> is not contagious. The cause of <span class="qt1">eczema</span> is unknown. It is likely caused by both genetic and environmental factors. <span class="qt1">Eczema</span> may get better or worse over time, but it is often a long-lasting disease. People who have it may also develop hay fever and asthma.</p><p>The most common type of <span class="qt1">eczema</span> is <span class="qt3">atopic</span> <span class="qt0">dermatitis</span>. It is most common in babies and children, but adults can have it too. As children who have <span class="qt3">atopic</span> <span class="qt0">dermatitis</span> grow older, this problem may get better or go away. But sometimes the skin may stay dry and get irritated easily.</p><p>Treatments may include medicines, skin creams, light therapy, and good skin care. You can prevent some types of <span class="qt1">eczema</span> by avoiding:</p><ul><li>Things that irritate your skin, such as certain soaps, fabrics, and lotions</li><li>Stress</li><li>Things you are allergic to, such as food, pollen, and animals</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Dermatologic disorders</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What does your skin do?<p>Your skin is your body's largest organ. It covers the entire outside of your body. There are many ways that your skin protects your body and helps keep you healthy. For example, it:</p><ul><li>Holds body fluids in, which helps prevent you from getting dehydrated</li><li>Keeps out harmful germs, which helps prevent infections</li><li>Helps you feel things like heat, cold, and pain</li><li>Helps control your body temperature</li><li>Makes vitamin D when the sun shines on it</li><li>Shields your body against heat and light</li></ul>What problems and conditions can affect your skin?<p>There are many different problems and conditions which can affect your skin. Some of them can cause uncomfortable symptoms, such as itching, burning, redness, and <span class="qt2">rashes</span>. They might also affect your appearance. Some of the more common skin conditions include:</p><ul><li>Acne, which causes pimples when hair follicles under your skin get clogged up</li><li>Burns</li><li>Cuts and scrapes</li><li>Dandruff, flaking of the skin on your scalp (the top of your head)</li><li><span class="qt1">Eczema</span> (<span class="qt3">atopic</span> <span class="qt0">dermatitis</span>), which causes inflammation, redness, and irritation of the skin</li><li>Hives, which are red and sometimes itchy bumps on your skin</li><li>Insect bites</li><li>Psoriasis, which causes itchy, scaly red patches</li><li>Skin cancer</li><li>Skin infections</li></ul>How can I keep my skin healthy?<p>Since your skin protects your body in many ways, it's important to try to keep your skin healthy. For example, you can:</p><ul><li>Wear the right protective equipment, like gloves, long sleeves, knee and elbow pads, or helmets to protect against cuts, bumps and scrapes.
</li><li>If you do get a cut or scrape, clean it right away with soap and warm water. Put on a bandage to protect it while it heals.
</li><li>When you are spending time outdoors, wear long sleeves and pants and use insect repellant to prevent insect bites.
</li><li>Prevent sunburn by covering up and using sunscreen when outdoors.
</li><li>Wash your hands often with soap and water.
</li><li>When you take a shower or bath, use warm (not hot) water. Use mild cleansers and wash gently (don't scrub).
</li><li>Use moisturizers, like lotions, creams, or ointments, to prevent dry skin.
</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases</p></content>
